name: Femi Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Femi, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at the copper pit outside town, and I lead the night crew on the trucks, eight drivers. Twelve-hour shift, start at six in the evening with the pre-start meeting, walk round truck 41 with a torch, check tyres, lights, oil. Then it's loop after loop: shovel, ramp, crusher, back down, about forty loads a night if the shovel's happy. Best part is about three in the morning when the radio goes quiet and it's just the lights on the benches.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What wears me out is the nights after the fourth one, when your body stops believing you. And the dust in summer, it gets into everything, even your sandwich. What I like is being trusted with a machine that weighs more than a house, and being the one the young drivers radio when they've got a soft spot on the ramp. My partner Joanna works nights at the district hospital too, so we eat breakfast together at seven and call it dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay. Honestly that sounds like most of what I hear already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so, at the crib room table. Half the toolbox talks this year have been about the future of mining, and nothing has changed on my truck except a new screen nobody reads. I'd probably put a joke in the crew group chat and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's a relief, because I don't want to learn some new system and I don't want to be the guy who can't. My job stays my job. I'd still keep one eye on the trucks, though, because the driverless haul fleets were never really about AI hype, they were already being tested before all this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much. I'd keep my shifts, keep putting the same bit into savings every fortnight, we're at about four months of bills now. Maybe I'd finally do the ticket for the bigger shovel that my supervisor keeps pushing, but probably I'd put that off again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like when the forecast says storm and it just rains a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the driverless trucks were being tested before all this. Where does that sit with you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a pit two hundred kilometres north where the trucks drive themselves already, and a mate of mine, Kofi's cousin, used to drive there. Now he sits in a control room in the city or he's gone, depending who you ask. So even if AI is hype, that's not hype, that's steel and GPS. In this picture it just doesn't spread to us, and I'd take that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say anything at the union meeting in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm a delegate, so yes, I'd say this is the time to lock in the agreement while the company isn't scared and isn't greedy. Get the redeployment clause written down while it costs them nothing. Joanna says I sound like my dad when I talk like that, and she doesn't mean it as a compliment.

S0.say: Told you so. Half the toolbox talks this year were about the future of mining, and nothing on my truck changed except a new screen nobody reads.
S0.think: It's a relief, because I don't want to learn a new system or be the guy who can't. The driverless trucks were being tested before any of this, so I'd still keep one eye on them.
S0.do: Keeps working the same night shifts and keeps saving at the same rate, at about four months of bills. Uses the quiet time as union delegate to push for a written redeployment clause, and probably puts off the bigger shovel ticket again.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, with a small leftover worry about the driverless truck fleets.
S0.quote: Even if AI is hype, that's not hype, that's steel and GPS.
S0.fieldNote: Femi splits AI into two things: the talk, which he dismisses, and the self-driving trucks at a nearby pit, which he treats as already real. His resistance to new tools is open and a bit proud. As a union delegate he'd use a calm period to lock in protections, which is his main way of acting on the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one I can actually see happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: if a machine takes the job, the people who did the job should share in what it saves. At work I'd be pushing that in every meeting. Online I'd stay quiet, I don't post much, but I'd share the union's stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, haul trucks are first in line. Trucks go loop after loop on a fixed road, that's exactly what they've already automated up north. Senior or not, best driver on the crew or not, a truck that never needs a tea break wins that argument with management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd get the union to demand a written plan: who goes to the control room, who gets moved to the shovels or the drills, how much notice. I'd stop putting off the shovel ticket and do it in the first six months, because shovels are harder to automate than trucks. And we'd stop talking about the new car and keep the old one another two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but it's there when I'm driving at three in the morning, wondering how many more nights there are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. If the control room jobs went to people who do, where does that leave you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Behind, probably. The kid on my crew, Dani, nineteen, she'd learn the control room screens in a week. I'd learn them in a month and hate every day of it. That's partly why I want the shovel ticket, I'd rather move sideways onto a machine than upwards into a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if the trucks went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners, not the robots. The copper price is good, they're not struggling. If they cut forty drivers to make the shareholders a bit happier, that's a choice, and the government lets them make it with no strings. I'd want a rule that says if you automate, you pay for the retraining, full stop.

S1.say: If a machine takes the job, the people who did the job should share in what it saves. I'd push that in every union meeting and share the union's posts, but I wouldn't post much myself.
S1.think: Haul trucks are first in line because they drive a fixed loop, the same work already automated at a pit up north. Being the best driver won't win that argument with management.
S1.do: Gets the union to demand a written plan on redeployment and notice. Takes the shovel ticket within six months because shovels are harder to automate, and keeps the old car two more years instead of buying new.
S1.feel: Anxious, especially on quiet night loops when he wonders how many nights are left.
S1.quote: I'd rather move sideways onto a machine than upwards into a screen.
S1.fieldNote: Femi's public line is about fairness and shared gains, while privately he knows his exact role is the easiest to automate. He chooses a sideways move to another machine over learning control room screens, which fits his dislike of new tech. He blames owners and weak rules, not the technology itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's two Christmases. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the government in on this now, not after. Somebody has to pay people when the companies don't need them. I'd be the one in the crib room reading the news out loud and making everyone listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished in this job, and I don't have a plan B that a robot can't also do. The shovel ticket doesn't help if the shovel drives itself too. Four months of savings feels like a lot until you divide it into the rest of your life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a fight over severance and a public income, that's the only thing that scales to everyone. We'd cut everything, cancel the holiday to the coast we booked for March. I'd probably talk to Joanna about moving in with her mum to stop paying rent, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being on the ramp when the brakes feel soft. You're still moving and you can't tell yet how bad it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning give you, compared to none?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Barely anything. Two years is the length of one enterprise agreement. Nobody retrains in two years into something that also isn't gone by then. Maybe it gives me time to save a bit more, maybe six months of bills instead of four, but that's a raft, not a boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Joanna that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we'll be fine, which would be a lie, and she'd know it. Her job is people, lifting people, talking to people, so maybe she'd last longer. That's a strange thing, me being the one depending on her. My dad would hate that, and I'm a bit ashamed that part of me hates it too.

S2.say: We need the government in on this now, not after, because somebody has to pay people when the companies don't need them. I'd be the one in the crib room reading the news out loud.
S2.think: I think I'm finished in this job, and I don't have a plan B that a robot can't also do. Four months of savings feels like a lot until you divide it into the rest of your life.
S2.do: Pushes the union to fight for severance and a public income. Cancels the March holiday to the coast, cuts all extras, and raises moving in with Joanna's mother to stop paying rent.
S2.feel: Like soft brakes on the ramp: still moving, with no idea how bad it is. Some shame about depending on Joanna.
S2.quote: Four months of savings feels like a lot until you divide it into the rest of your life.
S2.fieldNote: With two years, Femi sees no way out, because every option he'd accept is also automated. He looks to government and the union rather than to retraining. The admission that he's ashamed of depending on Joanna came out slowly and seemed to cost him something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better. Still not much better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, but louder and more organised. Five years is enough time to win a law if people start now. I'd tell the young ones on my crew to join the union the first week, not the first time something goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd see my own job go in slow motion. First the trial trucks, then half the fleet, then the night crew cut to three. I'd probably be one of the last drivers, because they keep the good ones to babysit the robots, and that's almost worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put twice as much into savings for the first two years and aim for a year of bills. I'd stand for the regional union committee, because that's where the deals get done. And I'd look at the government jobs, water, power lines, roads, places where you still need a person in a work truck for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The kind where I'd stop sleeping well on my days off, not just my nights on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're not keen on learning new things. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. If the union got a course paid for, I'd do it, I'm not stupid. But I'm not going to sit at home at night watching videos about AI on my own time. If they want me to learn, they pay me to learn, same as any ticket on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hold on to, money-wise, and what would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan's nearly done, so that stays. First to go is the fishing boat I've been looking at with my brother, we were going to go halves. Then eating out on our nights off. Joanna would say gym, but I'd fight for the gym.

S3.say: Five years is enough time to win a law if people start now. I'd tell the young ones on my crew to join the union in their first week, not after something goes wrong.
S3.think: I'd watch my own job go in slow motion, trial trucks first, then half the fleet. I'd probably be one of the last drivers, kept to babysit the robots, and that's almost worse.
S3.do: Doubles his savings for two years aiming for a year of bills, stands for the regional union committee, and looks at public jobs in water, power and roads. Drops plans to buy a fishing boat with his brother.
S3.feel: Alarmed, losing sleep even on days off.
S3.quote: They keep the good ones to babysit the robots, and that's almost worse.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Femi from defensive to organising: committee seat, savings goal, public sector jobs. He'll only learn new skills on paid time, which is both principle and reluctance. Being kept on as one of the last drivers is not a comfort to him, which surprised me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be idiots to waste it. Everyone should be at their MP's office now, before the companies write the rules for us. I'd say it calmly, which isn't my usual style.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years means I'd probably get eight more good years on the trucks or the shovel, and that's a lot of mortgage paid. But at the end of it there's nothing for me to switch to, because the end point's the same. I just get there older and with a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the shovel ticket, and I'd push the union to start a fund for drivers, like a strike fund but for this. We'd go ahead with buying a small place in town, because Joanna's job is steadier and rent just burns money. I wouldn't change careers in the first year, I'd wait and see where the trucks go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly, with a bit of something heavier underneath when I think about thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a house in this one. Isn't that a risk if the work goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But if everything's done by robots, rent's not getting cheaper either, and at least a house is ours. Joanna's mum bought her place on a nurse's wage in the eighties. We'd go small, two bedrooms near the hospital, nothing on the main street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared to the two-year picture, what changes most for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I've got nothing but anger. Ten years, I've got time to build something with other people, a fund, a law, a deal. I'm not changing who I am in ten years, I'll still hate screens. But I could make sure there's a floor under us when it lands.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift and we'd be idiots to waste it. Everyone should be at their MP's office now, before the companies write the rules for us.
S4.think: I'd probably get eight more good years on the trucks or the shovel, and pay down a mortgage. But the end point's the same, so I just get there older and with a house.
S4.do: Takes the shovel ticket, pushes the union to start a fund for displaced drivers, and buys a small two-bedroom place near the hospital with Joanna. Holds off on any career change in the first year to see where the trucks go.
S4.feel: Uneasy mostly, with something heavier underneath when he pictures himself at thirty-seven.
S4.quote: I'm not changing who I am in ten years, I'll still hate screens.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years turns Femi's anger into planning: a union fund, a house, a political push. He's clear that time won't change his dislike of technology, so his hope rests on a floor built by others, not on reinventing himself. He treats the house as a hedge against rising rents rather than a bet on his job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two years, easy. That one leaves no time for anything except being angry, and anger doesn't pay rent. What would help is a public income that kicks in the day the work goes, plus the companies paying into a retraining fund for every truck they automate, so it's not on us to work it out at night.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what the pit means to the town. Every football shirt in Redhill has the mine logo on it. If the trucks drive themselves, it's not just forty jobs, it's the bakery on Station Street and the school bus and the pub. Nobody in the city counts that.

headlineQuote: If they want me to learn, they pay me to learn, same as any ticket on site.
portrait: Femi Hansen is 27 and leads the night crew of haul truck drivers at a large copper pit, where he's also a union delegate. He lives with his partner Joanna, a night nurse, and has about four months of bills saved. He avoids new technology and never uses AI tools, and he'd rather move sideways onto a shovel than up into a control room. He dismisses AI hype but sees the driverless trucks already running up north as very real. Through the scenarios he leans on the union and government for answers, panics with two years of warning, and uses ten years to build a fund and buy a small house.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years leaves no time for anything except anger.
whatWouldHelp: A public income that starts the day the work goes, and companies paying into a retraining fund for every truck they automate.
